lessons.title: Data classes and shallow copies
lessons.summary: If copy instead receives topics = first.topics.toMutableList(), what prints?
explanation: A data class generates useful operations such as equals, hashCode and copy from properties declared in its primary constructor. Properties declared only in the body are excluded from those generated comparisons and copies. copy(topics = newList) replaces that constructor property in the new instance. toMutableList() copies a list container, but its element references are still shared.

copy creates another data-class instance but does not recursively clone referenced mutable objects. Here both instances retain the same MutableList reference. Read-only val prevents replacing the reference, not modifying that list.

Complete local Kotlin/JVM example; the app itself does not execute it:
```kotlin
data class Plan(val topics: MutableList<String>)
fun main() {
    val first = Plan(mutableListOf("C"))
    val second = first.copy()
    second.topics.add("Kotlin")
    println(first.topics.size)
}
```
Expected output or behavior: 2. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Sealed hierarchies and exhaustive when
lessons.summary: If label receives Waiting instead, what prints?
explanation: A sealed interface restricts its direct implementations to permitted declarations in the same package and module. It lets a when expression cover the known direct alternatives rather than relying on a catch-all branch.

data object declares a singleton alternative with data-style operations. A data class carries information for another case. In the is Ready branch, the smart cast exposes text; Waiting has only one named instance.

Complete local Kotlin/JVM example; the app itself does not execute it:
```kotlin
sealed interface State
 data object Waiting : State
 data class Ready(val text: String) : State
fun label(state: State): String = when (state) {
    Waiting -> "waiting"
    is Ready -> state.text
}
fun main() { println(label(Ready("done"))) }
```
Expected output or behavior: done. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Extensions use static resolution
lessons.summary: If item is declared Detail instead of Base, what prints?
explanation: fun Base.label() declares an extension with Base as receiver. It does not add an overridable member to Base or gain access to its private members.

When multiple extensions have the same name, selection uses the receiver’s compile-time type. A derived object held in a Base variable therefore uses the Base extension. Actual overridable members still dispatch dynamically; a matching member also takes priority over an extension.

Complete local Kotlin/JVM example; the app itself does not execute it:
```kotlin
open class Base
class Detail : Base()
fun Base.label(): String = "base"
fun Detail.label(): String = "detail"
fun main() {
    val item: Base = Detail()
    println(item.label())
}
```

lessons.title: Variance and projected access
lessons.summary: If first tries values.add(2.5) before returning values[0], what happens?
explanation: out T means a generic producer may expose T in output positions without accepting it as an ordinary input. This permits a Source<String> to be used as Source<Any>. in T supports the complementary consumer direction; variance does not mean deep immutability.

MutableList<out Number> is a use-site projection: it accepts a mutable list whose actual element type is some subtype of Number. Reading as Number is safe, but adding an arbitrary Number is not: the original list might allow only Int. The underlying list may still be mutated through another valid reference.

Complete local Kotlin/JVM example; the app itself does not execute it:
```kotlin
class Source<out T>(val value: T)
fun first(values: MutableList<out Number>): Number = values[0]
fun main() {
    val source: Source<Any> = Source("ok")
    val numbers = mutableListOf(3, 5)
    println(source.value)
    println(first(numbers))
}
```

Expected output or behavior: ok
3. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Inline reified type parameters
lessons.summary: If the checked value is 7 instead, what prints?
explanation: Most generic type arguments are erased on the JVM, so an ordinary generic function cannot simply ask value is T. inline with reified makes a function’s type parameter available for supported runtime operations at its call site.

inline fun <reified T> isA(value: Any): Boolean = value is T
fun main() { println(isA<String>("hello")) }

lessons.title: Close resources with use
lessons.summary: If the use block prints body then throws IllegalArgumentException(), what prints?
explanation: On the JVM, use runs a block with a closeable resource and closes it afterward, including when the block throws. Garbage collection is not a substitute for promptly closing files or similar resources.

import java.io.Closeable makes that JVM interface available by its short name Closeable. It defines close(). throw IllegalArgumentException() creates and throws an exception, transferring control rather than returning normally. The lambda passed to use runs before close; after runs only after use returns normally. A block failure is propagated after cleanup, so ordinary following code is skipped unless a suitable handler recovers.

Expected output or behavior: body
close

lessons.title: Result values and failure handling
lessons.summary: If the text becomes "twelve", what prints under this explicit fallback policy?
explanation: Result<T> holds either a successful T or a failure. runCatching executes a block and wraps any thrown Throwable as a failure. String.toInt() converts valid integer text but throws NumberFormatException when the text is not a valid Int representation; unlike toIntOrNull, it does not return null. It does not mean that every failure should be ignored or retried.

getOrElse returns the success value or calls a failure lambda for a fallback. The -1 fallback here is an explicit teaching policy. In coroutine code, blanket runCatching can capture cancellation exceptions too: do not silently convert cancellation into success; coroutine handling is taught separately.
